pll1d34c1-d1e3501.summary: Reports those who madly said that God's nature is not the same as the person or hypostasis, since the same essence could not be Father and Son without confusion; if the same thing is Father and Son, it begot itself. So they divide nature from person and do not accept that the one simple nature is three persons.
claims: Some separate the divine nature from the persons.

pll1d34c1-d1e3506.summary: Reports their appeal to Hilary, De Trinitate VIII, on Rom 8:9–11: the Spirit of God is the Spirit of Christ; Hilary asks whether 'Spirit of God' signifies the nature or a thing of nature, since nature is not the same as the thing of nature, as man is not what is man's, nor fire what is fire's, and so God is not the same as what is God's.
claims: Hilary says nature is not the same as the thing of nature.

pll1d34c1-d1e3551.summary: Replies that they do not understand Scripture's context: Hilary goes on to show that 'Spirit of God' sometimes signifies the Father ('the Spirit of the Lord is upon me'), sometimes the Son ('by the Spirit of God I cast out demons'), sometimes the Holy Spirit ('I will pour out my Spirit').
claims: 'Spirit of God' can signify Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.

pll1d34c1-d1e3594.summary: Cites Hilary's explanation: Christ dwells in us and God with him; the Spirit of Christ is the Spirit of God, a thing of one nature of Father and Son; the Spirit proceeds from the Father, is sent by the Son, and receives from him, since all the Father has is the Son's. So Christ is not anything other than God, one Spirit with God; 'I and the Father are one' teaches unity of nature, not the solitude of union.
claims: The Spirit of Christ and of God is one thing of one nature.
Christ is not other than God.
John 10:30 teaches unity of nature, not solitude.

pll1d34c1-d1e3638.summary: Notes that in these words the Spirit is called a thing of the nature of Father and Son, and is said to be God's nature, since through God's nature the nature itself dwells in us.
claims: The Holy Spirit is the divine nature.

pll1d34c1-d1e3641.summary: Concludes that in the Trinity one should not distinguish nature from thing of nature as in creatures, since, with Hilary, there is no comparison of earthly things to God, examples never contain the full reason, and one must not speak of God by human sense.
claims: Nature and thing of nature are not distinguished in God as in creatures.
Earthly comparisons do not fully apply to God.

pll1d34c1-d1e3665.summary: Interprets Hilary: he said 'nature is not the same as the thing of nature' looking to creatures and giving creaturely examples, then added 'and accordingly God is not the same as what is God's' to show the error of measuring the Creator by creatures; it would be impious to say God is other than what is God's, since God's Spirit and Son are God.
claims: Hilary's statement refers to creatures.
It is impious to say God differs from what is his.

pll1d34c1-d1e3686.summary: Cites Hilary's continuation: God's things are not to be understood in a bodily way. Man is somewhere and not elsewhere; God, immense power, is present everywhere and teaches himself wholly through his own, signifying that his own are not other than himself.
claims: God is everywhere and is not other than his own.
God is not to be understood in a bodily way.

pll1d34c1-d1e3700.summary: Explains: the divine nature is not other than what is its own and is in it, and through those it is in all its own that are not in it. Creatures are his but not in him; the three persons are his and in him, of and the same nature, as Augustine says: three persons of the same essence or the same essence, not from the essence.
claims: Creatures are God's but not in him.
The persons are God's and are the same nature.

pll1d34c1-d1e3707.summary: Grants a distinction by reason of understanding between hypostasis and essence, since the latter is common to three and the former is not; yet hypostasis is essence and vice versa. The three persons are one by essence and differ by properties.
claims: There is a rational distinction between hypostasis and essence.
Hypostasis is essence and essence hypostasis.
The persons are one by essence, distinct by properties.

pll1d34c1-d1e3710.summary: Cites Augustine on Ps 68: asked what the Father is, the Son, or both, answer 'God,' not 'gods'; the unity of substance admits equality but not plurality. If told the Son is the Father because he is what the Father is, answer that he is so by substance, not by what is said relatively.
claims: Each person and both together are God, not gods.
The Son is what the Father is by substance, not by relation.

pl-l1d34c1.summary: Refutes those who say God's nature is not the same as the person or hypostasis, arguing that one essence cannot be Father and Son without confusion, and who appeal to Hilary's 'nature is not the same as the thing of nature.' Read in context, Hilary shows that 'Spirit of God' sometimes means Father, Son, or Spirit, and that the Spirit of Christ and of God is one thing of one nature, so Christ is not other than God: unity of nature, not solitude. Hilary's distinction between nature and thing of nature applies to creatures, and Hilary warns that creaturely comparisons do not hold of God: God is not other than what is his, the persons being of and the same nature. There is a rational distinction between hypostasis and essence, since essence is common to three and hypostasis not, yet hypostasis is essence and vice versa; the persons are one by essence, differing by properties (Augustine on Ps 68).
claims: The divine nature is the same as the persons or hypostases.
Hilary's distinction between nature and 'thing of nature' applies to creatures, not to God.
The Spirit of God and of Christ is one thing of one nature, showing unity of nature, not solitude.
Creaturely comparisons do not hold perfectly of God.
God is not other than what is his own (the persons).
There is a rational distinction between essence (common) and hypostasis (not common), but hypostasis is essence.
The persons are one by essence and differ by properties.
